claim: WHO's 7 February 2024 epilepsy fact sheet reports around 50 million people living with epilepsy worldwide, nearly 80% living in low- and middle-income countries, up to 70% potentially becoming seizure-free with appropriate treatment, and about three quarters of people with epilepsy in low-income countries not receiving needed treatment.
method: Reviewed the WHO page's key facts, disease-rate section, treatment section, and WHO-response section. Recorded only the global burden, income-region distribution, treatment-gap framing, primary-care feasibility statement, and medicine-availability boundary that the page explicitly states.
limitations: The fact sheet provides global framing and does not supply a country- or district-level observed treatment cascade.
The three-quarters treatment-gap statement is framed for low-income countries and must not be silently generalized to all low- and middle-income countries.
The up-to-70% seizure-free figure is a potential outcome with appropriate diagnosis and treatment, not an expected result for every person or setting.

claim: WHO, the International League Against Epilepsy, and the International Bureau for Epilepsy published a global report that frames epilepsy care, treatment, research, and stigma reduction as public-health priorities requiring action at global, regional, and national levels.
method: Reviewed the WHO publication page and the linked English report description, including the stated purpose, collaborating organizations, and global, regional, and national response scope. Used the report for programme framing, not as a substitute for local prevalence or coverage data.
limitations: This is a global normative and evidence-synthesis report, not a current sub-national care dataset.
Its recommendations and country examples do not establish that a given delivery model will work in every health system.
The publication predates later medicine-access evidence and the 2022-2031 neurological-disorders action plan.

claim: WHO's 2024 report uses epilepsy and Parkinson disease as tracer conditions to describe medicine unavailability, unaffordability, and health-system barriers, and identifies national, subnational, district, programme, insurance, provider, and procurement decision-makers as intended users.

source.title: Improving access to medicines for neurological disorders

method: Reviewed the WHO publication overview and downloaded-report metadata for the tracer-condition choice, access-barrier framing, proposed multi-level action, and named policy and programme audiences. Classified this source as a measurement and decision-context source, not evidence that any particular intervention should be deployed.
limitations: The report describes system barriers and a framework for action but does not provide a harmonized observed epilepsy cascade for every country.
Epilepsy is used as a tracer for neurological-medicine access, so some findings are broader than epilepsy care alone.
The report cannot establish patient-level treatment effectiveness or local affordability without setting-specific data.

claim: A WHO/Health Action International analysis of facility-based surveys in 46 countries found that average public-sector availability of generic antiepileptic medicines was below 50% for all studied medicines except diazepam injection and that price and affordability varied substantially across income settings.

source.title: Mapping the availability, price, and affordability of antiepileptic drugs in 46 countries

method: Reviewed the PubMed abstract and article metadata for sampling frame, WHO/HAI survey method, five medicines studied, public and private availability, price ratios, and wage-based affordability measures. Treated the study as direct evidence about surveyed outlets and dates, not as a current global stock estimate.
limitations: The study is cross-sectional and its field data are old relative to the 2026 access date.
Facility and outlet availability does not prove procurement continuity, patient possession, adherence, or seizure control.
Phenobarbital data were available from only a small number of countries, and the five-medicine list is not the full modern antiseizure-medicine set.

claim: A 2022 cross-sectional survey of selected public, private, Red Cross, and community pharmacies in Addis Ababa found 52% overall availability of lowest-priced generic antiseizure medicines and reported that all available medicines were unaffordable under the study's wage-based method.

source.title: Availability, price, and affordability of antiseizure medicines in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia

method: Reviewed the open article metadata and abstract for the May 2022 field period, selected outlet counts, modified WHO/HAI method, generic availability, price ratios, and affordability calculation. Classified the study as a worked local measurement example that can inform a source inventory and measure dictionary.
limitations: Selected pharmacies in Addis Ababa do not represent Ethiopia nationally or other low-income countries.
A one-day outlet-availability measure does not show stock continuity, dispensing, patient possession, adherence, or clinical response.
The affordability result depends on the study's reference wage and standard-treatment assumptions.

claim: In a 24-cluster randomized trial in resource-limited communities in India, a home-based care model delivered by community and primary-care-equivalent workers improved antiseizure-medicine use and seizure outcomes compared with usual clinic care over 24 months, showing that a delivery model can be evaluated through observed adherence and seizure measures in one setting.

source.title: A cluster-randomized trial comparing home-based primary health care and usual clinic care for epilepsy in a resource-limited country

method: Reviewed the open article abstract and methods/results summary for cluster randomization, intervention components, 24-month follow-up, medication-use measure, seizure outcome, and attrition. Classified the result as evidence that a delivery pathway is testable, not as proof that the model should be scaled elsewhere.
limitations: The trial was conducted in one resource-limited Indian setting and cannot establish effects in other countries or health systems.
The intervention bundled medicine provision, home visits, adherence support, and education, so the causal contribution of any single component is not isolated.
COVID-19 affected part of the follow-up period, and the study population was identified through a local population survey rather than a national registry.

claim: The Global Burden of Disease Study 2021 estimated 51.7 million people with combined idiopathic and secondary epilepsy in 2021, using population-representative prevalence inputs and modeled estimates for 204 countries and territories.

source.title: Global, regional, and national burden of epilepsy, 1990-2021: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021

method: Reviewed the DOI-linked article record and open-access methods and results for the case categories, prevalence inputs, modeled estimation approach, geographic coverage, and 2021 global result. Classified this as a burden-framing source and preserved the distinction between modeled estimates and observed setting-level denominators.
limitations: The estimates are model outputs and do not provide an observed active-epilepsy denominator for a named district or facility catchment.
The study does not observe diagnosis, medicine stock, dispensing, possession, adherence, seizure control, referral, or follow-up continuity.
Input availability and case-definition harmonization can vary by location, so a country estimate is not a substitute for local ascertainment or linkage audit.

claim: A WHO Bangladesh summary reports a 2017 two-stage, population-based household survey of 10,080 people from 72 primary sampling units, with 9,839 respondents, an observed epilepsy prevalence of 8.6 per 1,000, and 66 of 85 confirmed cases classified as active epilepsy.

source.title: National Prevalence of Epilepsy Survey: Summary

method: Reviewed all three pages of the WHO South-East Asia Regional Office PDF for survey year, sampling frame, urban-rural allocation, response rate, prevalence denominator, active-epilepsy classification, treatment-gap calculation, and stated policy use. The PDF identifies the survey year but not an exact publication day, so the source date uses the schema's year-only convention.
limitations: The summary does not expose the full questionnaire, clinical confirmation protocol, or record-level data needed to reproduce every case classification.
The active-epilepsy and treatment-gap results use a small confirmed-case denominator of 85 and are not directly interchangeable with modeled estimates, clinic registers, or medicine-outlet surveys.
The PDF notes an imbalance in female participation among respondents under 18, and it does not provide longitudinal diagnosis, refill, referral, or seizure-control follow-up.
The PDF identifies the survey year but not an exact publication day; source_date uses the schema's year-only placeholder.

claim: A population-based rural South African study combined a cohort of 311 people with active convulsive epilepsy, questionnaire measures of diagnosis and health-facility contact, and blood antiseizure-medicine levels to characterize distinct care-cascade and adherence gaps.

source.title: Epilepsy care cascade, treatment gap and its determinants in rural South Africa

method: Reviewed the DOI-linked article record and open-access methods and results for the Agincourt population frame, active-convulsive-epilepsy case ascertainment, questionnaire stages, health-facility contact, blood antiseizure-medicine measurement, and treatment-gap definition. Classified it as a setting-specific cascade design example rather than a general LMIC estimate.
limitations: The study covers a rural South African surveillance area and cannot establish a national or cross-country cascade.
It focuses on active convulsive epilepsy and does not supply a complete pathway for all epilepsy types, referral completion, medicine stock continuity, or refill persistence.
Questionnaire responses, blood levels, and the surveillance catchment each have different missingness and selection mechanisms that must be retained in any replication.
The journal record identifies August 2020 rather than an exact publication day; source_date uses the first day of that month.

claim: A rural Ethiopian nurse-led epilepsy-clinic study used a clinic register and tracing of patients who met a predefined default criterion of three missed visits or at least six months without attendance, distinguishing death, migration, treatment from another source, remission, and ongoing seizures among traced defaulters.

source.title: Primary care treatment of epilepsy in rural Ethiopia: Causes of default from follow-up

method: Reviewed the DOI-linked article abstract and full methods and results for the rural health-centre catchment, register-based default definition, number of eligible and traced patients, tracing procedure, alternative treatment sources, seizure status, and reasons for default. Classified this as a longitudinal follow-up and loss-to-follow-up measurement example, not as evidence of current Ethiopian performance.
limitations: The study is from one rural health centre and its clinic register excludes people who were never diagnosed or registered and people receiving care elsewhere from the outset.
Only 113 of 165 identified defaulters were traced, and death causes and patient-reported reasons were not independently confirmed in every case.
The 1998-2005 care pathway and phenobarbital context are not current evidence about medicine availability, referral completion, or seizure outcomes in other settings.
The journal record identifies March 2009 rather than an exact publication day; source_date uses the first day of that month.

claim: WHO's 2023 Intersectoral global action plan on epilepsy and other neurological disorders establishes a 2022-2031 target and indicator framework spanning diagnosis, treatment and care, information systems, and public-health action, providing a policy reference for mapping a local epilepsy cascade to a named programme decision.

source.title: Intersectoral global action plan on epilepsy and other neurological disorders 2022–2031

method: Reviewed the official WHO PDF front matter, strategic objectives on timely diagnosis and treatment, research and information systems, public-health response to epilepsy, and the annex of targets and indicators. Used the plan to classify the policy and monitoring source family, not as evidence of local service coverage or intervention effect.
limitations: The action plan is normative and global; it does not provide observed country, district, facility, patient, or medicine-continuity data.
Its targets and indicators do not by themselves harmonize active-epilepsy denominators, diagnosis definitions, stock measures, possession, adherence, seizure outcomes, or referral completion.
The source cannot show that a local cascade artifact changes procurement or primary-care planning without field-reality review.
The publication record identifies the 2023 publication year rather than an exact publication day; source_date uses the schema's year-only placeholder.
